phonemes.desc: Short alpha with smooth breathing — the name opens clearly, without roughness.
Aspirated theta [tʰ], the sound of intellect: precise, sharp, clean.
Long eta with acute pitch — the stressed peak of the name, holding authority.
Long alpha with iota subscript, the old nominative ending that gives the name its archaic dignity.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-THAY-na' — the second syllable is pitched higher and drawn out; the final 'a' is long and pure.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Ἀθήνη (Athḗnē), the older epic form used by Homer — the long final alpha of Ἀθηνᾶ reflects the original stem

kin.label: Anatolian
kin.form: Attarsiya, a theophoric name borne by an Ahhiyawan leader in Hittite records (Indictment of Madduwatta), possibly related — the name may be Pre-Greek or Anatolian (Beekes)

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: no secure Indo-European etymology; proposals connecting the name to 'mind' or 'father' remain speculative

pronunciation.note: Athénā is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἀθηνᾶ contains both stress (acute on the long η) and length (η plus long alpha with iota subscript). The restoration Athénā preserves the acute stress; Athēnā is the macron-only variant. The form Athēnē changes the final letter and is used only when the domain requires it.

domains.title: The Grey-Eyed Strategist
domains.subtitle: Wisdom, Warcraft, Crafts, and Civilization
domains.lead: Athénā is unique among the Olympians: a warrior who fights only for just causes, a virgin goddess who needs no consort to validate her power, and the patron of the practical arts that make city life possible. She is intelligence made divine.

cards.name: Strategic Warfare
cards.desc: She favors counsel, discipline, and defensive battle over the berserk fury of Árēs; heroes like Odysseus and Diomedes fight under her sign.

cards.name: Wisdom and Counsel
cards.desc: The mind that sees all sides; her advice is practical, ethical, and far-sighted.

cards.name: Weaving and Crafts
cards.desc: Patron of weaving, pottery, carpentry, and olive cultivation — the technologies that sustain the polis.

cards.name: Guardian of Cities
cards.desc: Polias and Poliouchos: the goddess who protects the citadel and whose olive tree marks the land.

symbols.name: Owl
symbols.meaning: The night-eyed bird that sees through darkness — wisdom watching over the city; 'owl to Athens' was proverbial for something native and abundant

symbols.name: Olive tree
symbols.meaning: Her victory over Poseidon in the contest for Attica: food, oil, and wood in a single plant; the 'contest olive' on the Acropolis was shown to visitors into late antiquity

symbols.name: Aegis
symbols.meaning: The goatskin fringed with serpents and bearing the Gorgoneion, worn by Zeus and lent to Athena; at Troy it routs armies (Iliad 2.446–449)

symbols.name: Helmet and spear
symbols.meaning: Her warrior identity — always disciplined, defensive, and allied with just causes, never berserk

symbols.name: Gorgoneion
symbols.meaning: The apotropaic head of Medousa on her breastplate or aegis; the dead face that turns enemies to stone

symbols.name: Spindle and loom
symbols.meaning: Weaving as the emblem of ordered intelligence — and the arena of her contest with Arachnê

mythology.lead: Athénā's myths center on intelligence overcoming force. She is born from Zeus's head fully armed, defeats Poseidôn by gift rather than combat, and guides the heroes who win by cunning. Wherever she appears, calculation replaces rage.

myths.title: Born from the Head of Zeús
myths.text: Zeus, warned by Earth and starry Heaven that a son born to his first wife Mêtis — 'wisest among gods and mortal men' — would overthrow him, swallowed the pregnant goddess whole, a solution Hesiod calls Zeus's equal in cunning (Theogony 886–900, 924–929). The child, however, was a daughter. One day Zeus suffered a splitting headache, and the craftsman god — later sources name Hephaistos, some say Prometheus, the axe-stroke varies in the telling — cleft his skull, and Athena sprang forth 'from his immortal head,' fully armed, shaking a sharp spear, her cry so mighty that all heaven trembled (Theogony 924ff.; cf. Pindar, Olympian 7.35ff.; Homeric Hymn 28). She is thus the only Olympian with no mother in the ordinary sense: intelligence born directly from the sovereign mind, carrying both his cunning and the aegis that is his own. The myth makes her genesis an allegory — wisdom is what sovereignty produces when it swallows its own rival.

myths.title: The Olive Tree on the Acropolis
myths.text: Poseidon and Athena contested the land of Attica, and each gave the city a token: the sea god struck the rock of the Acropolis with his trident and a salt spring gushed forth (the mark was still shown in the Erechtheion in Pausanias's day); Athena planted the first olive tree, and Cecrops, the earth-born first king, judged her gift the better — food, oil, and firewood where the spring gave only brine (Pseudo-Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.1; Herodotus 8.55; Pausanias 1.24.5). Poseidon raged and flooded the Thriasian plain until the Athenians appeased him with honors — the joint shrine in the Erechtheion enshrines both tokens under one roof, a treaty in architecture. The Athenians told the story as their civic charter: the city chose the useful, the cultivated, the peaceable gift over the display of raw power. Civilization is the prize of a contest decided by judgment, not force.

myths.title: Arachnê Transformed
myths.text: The mortal girl Arachnê of Colophon — Ovid is our fullest teller, drawing on Greek sources now lost — was so fine a weaver that nymphs came to watch her, and when Athena herself descended in the guise of an old woman to warn her against rivaling the gods, Arachnê challenged the goddess outright. The contest they wove on adjacent looms is described in matching tapestries: Athena depicted the gods enthroned in glory and, in the corners, mortals struck down for hubris; Arachnê depicted the gods' own scandals — Zeus as a bull, as a shower of gold, as a swan — flawless work, and impious (Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.5–145). Three times Athena struck the web; then Arachnê, in shame, hanged herself, and the goddess in reluctant pity transformed her into the spider, weaver forever. The myth's edge is exact: skill without reverence is hubris, and hubris is punished even when it wins.

myths.title: Odysseus and the Long Return
myths.text: Athena's favorite mortal is the man 'of many turns,' and their partnership spans the Odyssey from beginning to end. She champions his return in the divine council (Odyssey 1.44–62), guides his steps invisibly, disguises him as a beggar on Ithaca, stands by his side through the slaughter of the suitors, and finally reconciles him to his people when vengeance threatens civil war (Odyssey 24.472–548). The pattern holds in the Iliad: it is Athena who restrains Achilles' hand and later drives his spear home against Hector, and who guides Diomedes' aristeia until the hero wounds Aphrodite and Ares themselves (Iliad 5.1–143, 846–909). Her bond with Odysseus is the closest thing in Greek myth to a partnership between human and divine intelligence — she loves him, the poem says, because 'he is so like-minded' with her. Wisdom does not replace effort; it steadies and crowns it.

myths.title: Athena and Perseus
myths.text: When Polydectes of Seriphos demanded the head of Medousa as a gift, Athena herself equipped the young Perseus for the impossible task, directing him to the Graiai and arming him with the polished shield in which he could watch the Gorgon's reflection without turning to stone (Pseudo-Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.4.2–3; Hesiod, Theogony 280 names Athena as guide of the hand that struck). From Medousa's severed neck sprang the winged horse Pegasos and the giant Chrysaor; Athena received the Gorgon's head and set it on her aegis, where its petrifying stare became the guardian of cities and the terror of Troy's fields. The motif recurs across her mythology: she arms the mortal, lends the shield, dictates the tactic — Perseus slays, Bellerophon rides, Heracles finishes the Hydra — but the plan is hers. Athena's warfare is the intelligence that makes force unnecessary, then supervises it anyway.

lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Athénā with Minerva, a goddess already associated with crafts and strategy, so the equation was unusually smooth; Minerva's temple on the Capitoline housed the guilds of artisans. In Egypt she was equated with Neith, the warrior-weaver goddess of Sais — Plato's Socrates remarks on the coincidence (Timaeus 21e) — and Hellenistic Jews identified her with Sophia, divine Wisdom. During the Renaissance she became the emblem of rational virtue and of learned institutions; in modern Athens she remains the namesake and symbol of the city, her helmeted head on coins and seals. The Parthenon, her temple, is the canonical image of Classical Greece and of ordered reason everywhere.
lore.culturalLegacy: Athénā is the divine patron of everything the Greeks most valued in civic life: wisdom, craft, disciplined courage, and strategic thought. The Athenian democracy claimed her protection; the Panathenaea, her great festival, processed the new peplos woven for her statue through the city, and the Parthenon frieze still shows it. In philosophy she became the emblem of reason; in art the model of dignified female power. Her owl, her olive, and her helmet remain instantly recognizable symbols of classical civilization, and her name crowns universities, academies, and a capital city. Restoring Athénā preserves the name under which the world's first democracy invoked its guiding intelligence.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Athénā is the goddess of the well-aimed blow — not merely in war, but in speech, craft, and thought. She does not rage; she calculates. She does not seduce; she advises. Her virginity is not a lack but a statement: her power is complete in itself, needing no alliance with masculinity to be effective.

In an age that often confuses intelligence with cleverness and power with dominance, Athénā offers a different model. She is strong because she is skilled, just because she is wise, and feared because she is right. The restoration of her name in Unicode is a small act of recognition: that wisdom, no less than beauty or wrath, deserves its original voice.
lore.archaeology: The Athenian Acropolis is her monument: the Parthenon (447–432 BCE) housed Phidias's colossal chryselephantine Athena Parthenos, known to us through ancient descriptions and the Varvakeion statuette copy; the Erechtheion preserved her olive tree, Poseidon's salt spring mark, and the archaic xoanon of Athena Polias dressed in the peplos; the little Ionic temple of Athena Nike guarded the citadel's approach. Phidias's bronze Athena Promachos stood between Propylaia and Parthenon for a thousand years. Every Panathenaic year, the prize amphorae of olive oil carried her armed image to victors across the Greek world — thousands survive. Beyond Athens, the temple of Athena Alea at Tegea (with pediments by Scopas), the archaic sanctuary at Lindos on Rhodes, and the great Hellenistic temples at Priene and Syracuse attest a civic cult older than the polis itself.
